s20.slug: SATURDAY · 7:50 PM · N. DUPRE STREET, MID-CITY — THE STEPS
body: Lena is asleep before Baton Rouge. Somewhere past the end of the Basin the weight goes off the back of Jack’s seat, and when he turns his head she is folded into the corner of the way-back against her window, directly behind him, her cheek on her own sleeve and her mouth a little open.

At Baton Rouge the interstate climbs a long steel bridge, and the Mississippi goes under them in the dark. It is wider than he had it in his head, black and moving, with lights on it: a towboat shoving a raft of barges upstream under one white lamp, the refineries strung out along the far bank, red lights blinking on the stacks. The water takes the lights and pulls them long downstream. Jack looks at it for the length of the bridge, and then twisted round in his chair, out the back glass past Lena asleep, until the levee closes over it.

After that an hour of dark, swamp on both sides of a road up on legs; the airport; New Orleans coming up on the right in a long low spill of orange; and Kevin at the wheel reading exits off Margot’s printout under his breath and taking the one for Carrollton.

N. Dupre Street is narrow and dark under its oaks, the sidewalks heaved into slabs by the roots, cars parked half up on the curb the length of the block. Half the porches are hung with black and gold. Somebody has painted a fleur-de-lis on a garbage can. The Broussards’ house sits up on piers at the top of a flight of wooden steps, long and narrow and running straight back from the street, the porch light on and the front door open behind the screen. In the side yard, under a work light clamped to the corner of a shed, a propane burner is going with a sound like a jet that has decided to stay, and the steam off a pot the size of an oil drum goes up white through the light and into the branches. Back there somewhere a radio: WWL, a man and a woman talking over each other about precincts, and the polls about to close.
Kevin brings the Odyssey in against the curb behind a pickup with WHO DAT soaped across its back glass, puts it in park, sets the brake and turns off the engine. In the quiet the burner roars.
“Thirty-five hours and forty minutes,” Kevin says. “Theo.”

body.text: “Within tolerances,” says Theo, already out his door.
body.else: “Approximately,” says Theo, already out his door.

body: The doors come open on both sides and the night comes in, cool and damp, boiling spice off the yard and a sweetness on the air from somebody’s bush that Jack doesn’t have a name for. Margot gets out holding her maps. Laney climbs over the bench from the way-back, stiff in every joint, and stops with one boot on the step to look down at Lena, who hasn’t moved.
“She sleeps like she’s being paid for it,” Laney says.

Jack gets her out without deciding to. He has her duffel up off the floor and over his shoulder, and then he is in between the chairs on one knee with an arm under her knees and the other behind her back, and she comes up off the bench all at once, warm from sleep and heavier than she looks, and her head drops into the hollow under his collarbone and settles. The pencil slides out of the knot at the back of her head, and her hair comes down over his arm. She says something into his shirt that isn’t a word. He backs out of the van with her, and on the sidewalk the others stand with their bags and let him by.

The steps go up a full story to the porch, steeper than steps have any business being, built by somebody who expected water. He takes them one at a time with her weight against his chest and the duffel knocking at his hip. Somewhere around the middle he hears the pencil go down them behind him, step by step, into the dark. In her sleep her hand has found a fistful of his shirt front, and it doesn’t let go.

Her mother is in the door. Jack has never laid eyes on her and would know her anywhere: Lena’s chin and Lena’s eyes, thirty years on and tired, in blue scrubs from a shift at Touro with a cardigan over them and one hand holding the screen door wide. She watches him come up her stairs with her daughter. Her face does nothing, and everything.
“Second door on the left, baby,” she whispers, and stands back to let them in.

The hall runs straight back through the house, room opening off room, every light on, the smell of the boil coming down it from the yard. The second door on the left is a narrow room with a twin bed under a crucifix and a Saints pennant from 1987, the felt gone soft as a dish towel. Somebody has turned the bed down. He lays her on it, and she turns her face into the pillow and is gone again.
“Boots,” Celeste whispers from the doorway.
He works her Justins off, heel and toe, and sets them side by side under the bed, and puts the duffel at the foot of it, and backs out of the room past her mother.

Out on the porch the others have come up with the bags and are standing in a row by the swing, Margot with Gloria’s white box held upright in both hands. In the swing sits a small old woman in a housedress and a gray cardigan, with the tail of a rosary hanging out of the cardigan pocket and her feet not quite reaching the boards.

body.text: “*Le garçon de l’Ohio.*” It is a voice he knows from three phone calls, and it comes out of a much smaller person than he had built for it.
body.else: “*Le garçon de l’Ohio.*” It is a voice he knows from two phone calls, and it comes out of a much smaller person than he had built for it.

body: She looks at his empty hands, and up at his face.
“Yes, ma’am.”
Theo steps up beside him with his overnight bag on his shoulder and the smile he keeps for other people’s mothers. “Madame Broussard. Theo Vance. I’ve taken the liberty of —”
“You sleep here.”
“Yes, ma’am.”
Behind him Laney mouths *I told you* at the back of his head.

Mémère puts one foot down and stops the swing. “Boys in the attic. Girls downstairs, with Magdalena and them. And me, I sleep in the front room.” She tips her head at the window behind her, where a lamp is lit beside a made-up daybed. “Where I can see the stairs.”
Going back down for Kevin’s cooler, Jack finds Lena’s pencil on the third step from the bottom and puts it in his shirt pocket.
Inside, at the foot of the attic stairs, Celeste stops him with a hand on his sleeve. She keeps her voice at a whisper that carries exactly as far as he is.
“She doesn’t sleep in cars,” she says. “Since she was little. She’d stay up all the way to Lafayette.”

journal.title: Celeste Broussard
journal.text: Lena’s mother. A nurse at Touro. Gives her orders in a whisper. Saturday night she was in the door when I came up her steps with Lena asleep. Second door on the left, baby.

journal.title: Odile Broussard (Mémère)
journal.text: Lena’s Mémère. Breaux Bridge. Eighty-eight. The monks’ fruitcake came; it’s *trop sec*; she’s eating it anyway. Prayed for Wes at the eight o’clock. *Quelqu’un devait demander.* Asked for le garçon de l’Ohio. Wes told her I’m skinny. I said oui, madame. She says I have manners. The Friday before I flew back she took the phone for ten seconds to ask was I eating. When I come to New Orleans I come to her house first. Thursday at seven in the morning she called me herself, from Dupre Street, on a number the redhead gave her. She knew I’d said yes. She called anyway: I don’t come because the rich boy asked me, I come because she asked me. Don’t bring nothing. Come to this house first — I said it back to her. Lena told her not to call. Saturday night on the porch she cancelled Theo’s hotel. You sleep here. Boys in the attic. She sleeps in the front room, where she can see the stairs.

journal.title: Kevin Tran
journal.text: Kevin Tran. Goes to daily Mass, saves you a seat with a Bible. Has a sister, Tina, in dental school, who flossed in the womb. Lies to his mom about orgo in Vietnamese. Drives his mother’s Odyssey at sixty-five, not sixty-six. His dad has two nail-salon supply stores in San Jose and has never had a Labor Day. Brought six pairs of gloves to a beach cleanup. Mouthed every word of Joey’s first reading from the second pew. Somebody coached Joey; I can guess who. Brought tea to a wake. His Bà Nội says heaven makes the elephant and heaven makes the grass. Walked Margot down at four in the morning. Handed Lena a roll of quarters for the payphone before she asked. Halloween: All Saints, every one nobody’s heard of — scrubs, a halo and a white mask. He found Laney. Friday night a pre-med said Maine got it right. Kevin answered him and went to get water. Tuesday, the Vietnamese Martyrs: his mother reads eleven of the hundred and seventeen. Asked about the scar. Alarm Five, on the lawn: he had a question mark next to my name on his clipboard. I told Priya I was out. He erased it. Tuesday at four I woke him for Doug. A chair under the knob, then a bell. Wednesday at the Brick, at the next carrel all night: ‘You two have been defending each other for three hours. That isn’t studying.’ Sings bass. A real one. Seven years of Vietnamese choir in San Jose — his mother made him. Friday, from the Odyssey: Go home. Sleep. Tell somebody something. Back from San Jose. His mother has a girl from their parish she wants him to call. Clare. She plays the violin in the Mass band. Wednesday he brought two flats of water to the Haiti table, which nobody asked for, and stayed to hold Clare’s violin case. ‘My mother knows your mother.’ Thursday he called Clare. His mother had the number, and his grandmother was on the speaker. She said yes to Sully’s. MLK Day he brought gloves for everybody. Tuesday in the basement he read us the first reading off his BlackBerry. Clare’s going to the Walk for Life, and so is he. He asked me to come — for him. I said yes. Thursday at the window table he had a list: things to say at hour four. He’d heard about Hale’s — Laney to Margot to him — and didn’t take a side. Then he asked me what you’re supposed to feel at hour four. I told him. He wrote it down. Clare asked him which of us was right at Hale’s; he told her he didn’t have the information, and she said that was a very Kevin answer. He asked if my brother’s okay. Thursday night at the van he had a clipboard and a seating chart taped to the dash, and said he’s pre-med, not a switchboard. Clare came to see him off. At three in the morning he was at St. Brendan’s ahead of me. Couldn’t sleep either. At a quarter to five Osei blessed his mother’s car again. Still pretty blessed. Friday under the dinosaurs at Cabazon he told Theo and Laney to leave it alone. He checked the oil at the Arizona line. He called Clare from El Paso, like he said he would. He kept the clock the whole way: thirty-five hours and forty minutes.

choices.text: “She fell asleep at Baton Rouge, ma’am. She was up all night navigating.”
choices.key: On Dupre Street you carried Lena up her mother’s steps, asleep. Celeste said she doesn’t sleep in cars. You told her Lena was up all night navigating.
response: “Was she.” Celeste looks past him down the hall at the second door on the left, and back at him, and whatever she thinks of it she keeps. She takes the cooler out of his hands and gives it to Remy, who has appeared from nowhere to be given it, and turns Jack by the elbow toward the back of the house. “Tony’s in the yard. Go on. He’s been waiting on you all day.”

choices.text: “Kevin has a rule about nobody getting carried. I’m going to hear about it.”
choices.key: On Dupre Street you carried Lena up her mother’s steps, asleep. Celeste said she doesn’t sleep in cars. You told her Kevin has a rule about nobody getting carried.
response: Celeste laughs, a whisper of one, mostly air, and puts her hand over her mouth to keep it from reaching the second door on the left. “The little one with the clipboard? I’ve heard about him.” She takes the cooler away from him. “Go out back, baby. Tony’s in the yard. He’s been waiting on you all day.”

choices.key: On Dupre Street you carried Lena up her mother’s steps, asleep. Celeste said she doesn’t sleep in cars. You told her you didn’t think about it. No, she said. I saw.
response: She lets go of his sleeve and points him down the hall toward the yard, the light and the noise, and goes back up the hall the other way, without hurrying, to look in at the second door on the left.

s21.slug: SATURDAY · 8:05 PM · DUPRE STREET, THE SIDE YARD — THE BOIL
body: In the side yard the work light makes a room out of the dark: the low arm of the oak overhead, the board wall of the shed, a picnic table, a cooler, a folding lawn chair with a cushion on it, and in the middle of it the burner, roaring blue under the pot. Over the pot stands Tony Broussard with a paddle the size of an oar. He is fifty-three and big, gone soft in the middle and hard everywhere else, in a BROUSSARD’S SEAFOOD · BANKS ST. T-shirt under an open flannel, with steam in his eyebrows. A mesh sack of crawfish slumps against the cooler, alive and rustling, small and dear this early in the season, and in the red water corn and new potatoes and garlic by the head go round and round.
He sees Jack and leans the paddle on the rim and comes around the pot with his hand out. It is a fish market’s hand, wet and enormous, and he looks Jack over while he shakes.
“The Ohio boy.”
“Yes, sir. Jack.”
“Browns?”
“Yes, sir.”
Tony shuts his eyes. “Lord, son.” He opens them again on the van at the curb. “Thirty-five *hours*? In a *Honda*?”
“It’s an Odyssey, sir,” says Kevin, coming through the side gate with an armful of sleeping bags. “It’s a very good car.”

Tony looks at Kevin, and at the van, and back at Kevin, and goes back to his paddle, stirring from the bottom with his back in it. “You hear what the league did to us? Sent lawyers. *Lawyers.* To T-shirt men. A man on Decatur with a card table and his kids’ tuition in a cigar box, and they send him a letter says *Who Dat* is theirs.” He knocks the paddle on the side of the pot. “So the senator writes them a letter back, and the attorney general got in it, and they quit. Course they quit. You can’t own what a city hollers. Who’s it belong to, the man selling the shirt, or the man in section whatever since nineteen eighty-one? And before that with a bag on his head.”

Ten minutes after that the paddle is in Jack’s hands, and he couldn’t say how. Tony said, “Here, hold this,” and went in the shed for the corn, and came back with the corn and without any interest in the paddle. “From the bottom,” he says, over Jack’s shoulder. “Like you mean it.” He reaches past him and punches the radio off in the middle of a woman saying *turnout* and puts a tape in the boombox on the shed’s windowsill, and a piano comes rolling out of it, slow and easy, and a voice like gravel in cane syrup. “Enough of that. They can call it without me.”
After that the family comes in waves, out the back door and down the back steps into the light, and every one of them already knows who he is.

Remy first, twenty, an LSU cap on backward and a beer in his hand, who grabs Jack’s free hand over the paddle and pumps it. “Brother-in-law!” He is very pleased with this. Tony doesn’t tell him to stop.

Luc comes after him, the oldest, off duty, compact in a Saints sweatshirt and a haircut that says cop from across the yard, who shakes his hand once and says, “Luc,” and takes up a place against the fence with a can of Barq’s. From there he can see the gate, the pot, the back door, and Jack. He watches all four.

Tess is next, with Beau behind her carrying a diaper bag and a folding chair, and in the crook of her arm a bundle in a black-and-gold knit cap, seven weeks old and asleep through all of it. Tess looks at Jack over her daughter’s head with frank interest, the way you look at a man you might be about to put to work.

The twins come at a run, thirteen, in Saints shirts down to their knees. Josie stops dead in front of the pot. She has Lena’s eyebrows and Lena’s way of standing with her weight on one hip, ready for a fight.
“Are you the Ohio boy?”
“Yes.”
“You’re not the violin.”
“No.”
“*Good.*”
She walks off. Jude doesn’t say anything. He steals a potato out of the colander on his way past and eats it hot, blowing on his fingers.

When Celeste comes out on the back steps, changed out of her scrubs, Laney is at the bottom of them. Celeste stops two steps up and looks at her: the copper hair, the quilted vest, the face that has been unspeakable since San Antonio.
“So *you’re* my redhead.”

And Laney Price, who has called this woman every night for a week, bursts into tears. Celeste comes down the last two steps and gathers her in, and Laney cries into the front of her cardigan for no reason she gives anybody, and Celeste rubs her back in small slow circles between the shoulder blades, a nurse’s circles, and says, “I know, baby. I know,” over the top of her head.

Margot has been given the corn, a step stool and a garbage bag for the husks, and shucks with her sleeves shoved up to the elbow, ruthless and quick, looking happier than Jack has seen her since Big Sur. Kevin has been fed twice: once by Celeste, a bowl of something from the stove inside, and once by Mémère, who did not see the first bowl and would not have believed in it. Mémère herself has been installed in the lawn chair with a jelly glass. Theo is down on one knee beside it, charming her. She lets him finish, and says something in French to the twins, and the twins fall about. Theo regroups and charms her again, slower, and this time at the end of it she hands him her glass to hold while she gets her rosary untangled from her pocket. He fails better.
Tony is at Jack’s elbow with a jelly glass of his own, amber, a curl of lemon peel riding in it and the smell of licorice coming off it from a foot away. He holds it out to him across the burner.
“Sazerac. I make them myself. Rye whiskey, Peychaud’s, a little sugar, the Herbsaint just to wet the glass.” The glass hangs there in the steam. “You drink, son?”

journal.title: Tony Broussard
journal.text: Lena’s father. Broussard’s Seafood, Banks Street. Twenty-eight years in the same seats. Held the phone up to the kitchen radio for the whole second half while we lost him at every curve on Highway 1. Wes told him there’s a Browns fan out here. Laney had him at hello. Saturday night in the side yard he put me on the paddle inside ten minutes. Thirty-five hours, in a Honda. Lord, son.

journal.title: Laney Price
journal.text: Laney Price. Pi Lam, as of Thursday: ran back across Seacliff in a pink cowboy hat to Lena first. The night before, on the floor of 217 in a white dress, she asked what happens if they look at her and see. First Catholic Mass: arms crossed like a Baptist, came back from the blessing pink and quiet. Programmed herself into my phone. (Hoodie status: hers.) Pi Lam’s barn party: carried upstairs by her new sisters, glorious and wrecked. Called Lena a mother over the banister. Said sorry at the sign of peace, at her second Mass. Big/Little: Sloane is her big. On the front steps at one in the morning, in a PI LAM LITTLE shirt, with a balloon on her wrist, she told me about Kaylee Whitmore. Fifteen; Kaylee drove; they’d both been drinking and Laney let her. Preston Road. A culvert. A cast for six weeks that everybody signed. A month later, a doctor’s note for flying; she’d never been on a plane. Lena’s the only other one who knows. In the water at Pfeiffer Beach she caught my swan. It’s Theo’s. Her fourth Mass, up a mountain with the monks. Asked Lena how you light a candle, and lit one. Don’t you dare, she said. Halloween: Pope Joan, in a cardboard mitre with gold rickrack. Blessed Del Playa from the widow’s walk until Rafi’s father asked her to come down. Over a bullhorn. Best Couple, with Margot. Went missing with three pledges for most of the extra hour; Kevin found her at Lupe’s with a burrito. She’s not stupid. She’s hungry. Friday at the Situation Room: ‘Who’s that?’ ‘No one.’ Alarm Five: ‘Fireman. You’re dressed.’ Saturday on the laundry table with Theo and a legal pad, discussing finals. Somebody put an orange in her Ugg. She’s crying. The Advent party: black velvet, in mourning for Advent. A Texas thing in the punch; Kevin took her flask. Asleep on the porch swing by a quarter to eleven. The ninth at nine at the Anchor, with an agenda on an index card: pie, no questions. Sunday night she came out of my room with her laptop and went past me without a word. Since Sunday she hasn’t said a word to me. At the Haiti table she met Skye, and gave a hundred dollars to the clipboard. Wednesday night in the lounge she was keeping it short with Theo, for a nod. Then, to me, without turning her head: ‘Night.’ At Sully’s Skye brought her a present. She wore her own bells. She gave Skye advice, and I told her I’ve seen her work. Then she took a shot at Skye, and Skye was handling it, and I didn’t let her. I’ve never yelled at Laney before. The whole bar heard. Tuesday, after the storm, she came back down to the laundry room by herself, with a list: the airport, the status, Sully’s, the jacket, me. She asked what I’m doing. I told her the truth, which I haven’t told anybody. Then I left her standing there. I’m done with that room. Both of them. Friday on the west stairs she and Theo were doing a bit at each other about memory. I said morning. In the lounge she died across the arm of the couch over a picture of tacos. Then she looked at me a long time. Monday night she and Theo were on the lounge floor with two legal pads side by side, and turned them over when I came in. A wedding seating chart, Theo said. Hypothetical. She took ink off my face with her thumb, and went cold again. Thursday night at the van she said she wasn’t Western Union and relayed everything anyway. She packed me a bag: FIREMAN, LARGE. Thirty hours. Behave. She told me Julian isn’t coming, like I’d care, and I told her so. Friday night in El Paso she broke a pill in half with her thumbnail. It’s a prescription, Theodore. Saturday on Dupre Street Lena’s mother said So you’re my redhead, and Laney cried in her arms and didn’t say why.

choices.text: “Abita, sir, if it’s the same to you.”
choices.key: In the side yard Tony put you on the paddle and held out a Sazerac. You asked for an Abita. He allowed it.
response: “It’s not the same to me,” Tony says. “But I’ll allow it.” He drinks the Sazerac himself in two swallows, digs an Abita out of the ice, knocks the cap off on the edge of the picnic table and puts the cold bottle in Jack’s free hand.

He takes the paddle back. He looks into the pot, and at the sky, and at his watch, and turns around to his yard and his family and half of Dupre Street, and his voice goes up over the piano and the burner both: “*Dump it!*”

choices.key: In the side yard Tony put you on the paddle and held out a Sazerac. You drank it. It was very strong.
response: It is very strong. It goes down like a lit match and keeps going, rye and licorice and sugar, and the back of his throat shuts and his eyes run, and Remy, overjoyed, pounds him on the back.

Tony watches him get it down, satisfied about something, and takes back the paddle. Jack is still holding the jelly glass with a finger of it left in the bottom when Tony turns to the yard, fills his chest, and roars: “*Dump it!*”

choices.key: In the side yard Tony put you on the paddle. You said you’d have whatever Mémère was drinking. Mémère was drinking a Sazerac.
response: Mémère is drinking a Sazerac. It is very strong. Tony is so pleased he has to set the paddle down; he gives Jack his own glass and pours himself another out of a pitcher on the cooler, and across the yard Mémère lifts hers at Jack from the lawn chair, and Jack lifts his back, and drinks, and the edges of the yard go soft.
Tony cups both hands round his mouth and turns toward the back steps: “*Dump it!*”

s21a.slug: SATURDAY · 8:45 PM · DUPRE STREET, THE TABLE — THE SEAT
body: Tony and Luc lift the basket out of the pot between them, streaming, and walk it to the long table Beau and Remy have made out of two sawhorses and a door under the work light, laid with three thicknesses of the *Times-Picayune*, and upend it down the middle: a red landslide of crawfish, corn, potatoes split by the heat, garlic gone soft in its skins, and a few blue crabs from the market boiled orange. The steam goes up into the light. For a second everybody stands and looks at it, and then everybody sits.

Celeste points Jack into a chair halfway down the far side — “There, baby” — and goes for paper towels. Margot has the chair on one side of him. On the other side the bench at the end of the table is empty.

He has been in the chair about a minute when Tess comes round behind him and puts her daughter in his arms. “Hold her for me, I need a hand,” she says, and takes the hand back to her own place and uses it to eat, and doesn’t come back for the baby. Lucille weighs about what a sack of flour does and is a great deal warmer. She sleeps in her black-and-gold cap with one fist up by her face, and when he shifts her into the crook of his left arm she opens her mouth and thinks about crying and doesn’t.

Margot has kept Gloria’s white box out of the twins’ reach all evening, on top of the refrigerator, and now she brings it out and sets it down on the newspaper in front of him, since it’s his to answer for.

body.text: Mémère sees it from the head of the table: the white box, and on the lid Gloria’s 5, ringed twice in ballpoint. “You brought something.”
body.else: Mémère sees it from the head of the table: the white box, and purple coming through at one corner of the cardboard. “You brought something.”

body: “It’s from a woman who’s been on her feet thirty years, ma’am,” Jack says, over the baby. “She says you don’t walk into somebody’s house empty-handed.”
Mémère holds her hand out without taking her eyes off him. Celeste puts a fork in it, and cuts a sliver from the edge of the pie with a butter knife, and passes it up the table on a paper towel.

body.text: Mémère eats it slowly. “*Bon.*” She gives the fork back to Celeste and says to her, in French, not low: “*Il a pas écouté.*” And Celeste looks down the table at Jack.
body.else: Mémère eats it slowly. “*Ça tache.*” She finishes it anyway. “*Bon.*”

body: Julian’s box comes next. Celeste brings it out of the house and sets it at her own place and unties the twine both ways with quick competent fingers, and folds back the brown paper. Inside, on a bed of tissue, is a CD in a sleeve lettered by hand, FOR LUCILLE, and under it, smaller, *songs for going to sleep*; and an envelope in the same careful upright hand, to Mrs. Broussard. Celeste reads the card to herself. She holds up the CD and turns it round so the table can see.
“*Le petit violon*,” Mémère says, approving.
“That boy,” says Celeste, and puts the card in her cardigan pocket.
Tony takes the CD from her and turns it over and reads the back, and shakes his head over it in admiration. “Now *that’s* a son-in-law.”

The CD goes from hand to hand down the newspaper, and everybody has a good word for it, and Jack sits in the chair Celeste put him in with Lucille asleep against his arm, and not one person at the table finds anything to correct. He takes a crawfish off the pile with his free hand and tries to peel it one-handed. It comes apart in three pieces, and something hot squirts him in the eye.
“You’re doing it wrong,” Josie tells him, from across the table.

Forty minutes in, the screen door bangs and Lena comes down the back steps into the light in a purple LSU sweatshirt that has to be Remy’s, the sleeves down over her hands, sleep on her face and her hair flat on one side and loose on the other. Lucille has started to fuss, and Jack is on his feet handing her back across the table to Tess when Remy slides into his chair behind him.
“Thank you, brother-in-law.”

Lena drops onto the end of the bench beside it. And without looking, she reaches back and takes a fistful of the back of his shirt and pulls him down onto the bench next to her, as if it were always his seat.
The table registers it, and keeps eating. Across the shells Theo’s eyes go to Laney, and Laney’s are already on Theo, and both of them find something urgent to do with the corn.
Lena reaches over and takes her pencil out of his shirt pocket, and twists her hair up off her neck, and puts the pencil through it. She looks at what he has done to the crawfish on his paper towel.

“Lord have mercy.” She takes a fresh one off the pile, puts it in his hands and puts her hands over his. Hers are hot from the pile, and slick with it, and quick. “Pinch.” Her thumbs on his thumbs, at the joint where the head meets the tail; there’s a split at the side of his thumbnail, and the cayenne finds it, and so does she. “Twist.” The head comes off. “Now the end of the tail, there. Squeeze. Pull.” The meat slides out in one piece, pink and curled, and she takes her hands back and takes the tail out of his fingers and eats it herself.
While he is doing the next one on his own she steals the potato off his paper towel.

body.text: When Tony comes by with the pitcher she takes the jelly glass out of Jack’s hand, finishes what’s in it, and gives him back the empty. “Daddy makes them for Louisiana,” she tells him.
body.else: Halfway down the pile she takes his Abita from beside his elbow and drinks from it, a long pull, without asking, and puts it back where it was with the label turned the way he had it.

body: Tony leans down the table on his forearms. “Thirty-five hours, cher. In a Honda.”
“We did thirty-five hours,” Lena says, peeling. “Kevin has the clock.”
Jack keeps his eyes on his crawfish. Under the table her knee comes over against his, and it stays.

body.text: The pie box sits open on the newspaper with two slivers gone. Lena looks at the lid, at the 5 ringed in Gloria’s ballpoint, a second longer than a lid needs.

body: There are blue crabs on the paper, boiled orange, and Rosie asked for a report. Jack wipes his fingers on his jeans and gets the RAZR out.
Lena is reading over his arm without asking. “*Procambarus clarkii*,” she says, and points at the pile with a tail. “Tell her a girl from New Orleans said.”
He does.

body.text: procambarus clarkii. a girl from new orleans said

body: He sets the phone down face-up on the newspaper by their two paper towels, with Ma’s line on the screen, and Lena reaches across it for another crawfish.

journal.title: The Anchor
journal.text: Marionberry: 4/10. Olallieberry: 9/10 — Dad would eat two pieces and complain about the second. Gloria rated Lena: pecan. She rated Margot without meeting her: rhubarb — tart, and nobody can decide if it’s a fruit. She rated Becca without meeting her: apple. Honest crust. Nobody loses sleep over an apple. Then she asked what happened to the pecan. A whole pie for a funeral is half price. I work here Tue/Thu/Sat, seven to one. Once a year the kitchen goes dark on a Thursday. Saturday the 10th Gloria met Becca: ‘Apple. Told you, hon.’ She looked at Wes a long time. ‘Peach.’ Everybody likes a peach, she says. Saturday the 12th: boysenberry, for a girl off the TV. Sweet up front, tart after. It stains. Saturday on Dupre Street Mémère tasted Gloria’s pecan off a fork. *Bon.*

journal.title: Rosie
journal.text: Rosie Costigan, eight. Drew Theo as a prince before she ever met him. Drew him again in Dad’s parka. He kept both. Christmas Eve she said grace — the baby in New Orleans, Danny, Nonna’s hand, Theo’s mom’s coach. Christmas night she drew the TV girl, with me and a crab. Rosie’s midnight is at nine, off a tape Dad made in 1999. Pots and pans on the porch. Asleep by a quarter past with the spoon. Counted her New Year’s lentils out like coins. Put the three kings at the manger on the sixth. Drew me a plane with the crab in the next seat. Saturday from New Orleans, for her list: *Callinectes sapidus*, confirmed. *Procambarus clarkii* — a girl from New Orleans said. Rosie says thank the girl.

s22.slug: SATURDAY · 9:15 PM · DUPRE STREET, THE KITCHEN TABLE — LANDRIEU
body: Celeste sends the two of them inside with the leftover tails and two mixing bowls — “For tomorrow. Peel, don’t eat” — and they end up side by side at the kitchen table, shelling for the game, her elbow knocking his every time she reaches for the bowl and him not moving over, with WWL on the little television on the counter by the bread box and the sound turned up.

It is the kitchen he drew in his head on the phone on Thursday, nearly: the black iron pot on the back burner, the cayenne in its tin beside the stove. He drew fewer saints. There is one on the windowsill, one on the refrigerator with a magnet through his halo, and St. Jude on a calendar from the parish, still turned to January. Tony stands at the head of the table with a dish towel over his shoulder. Luc leans on the counter with his arms crossed. In the doorway from the hall Mémère has set herself up in a kitchen chair with her jelly glass, where she can see the television and the stairs both.

On the screen the numbers come up in a box in the corner, and the two anchors keep saying the same thing in different words: it’s over. Landrieu has it outright, about two votes out of every three, no runoff. They cut to his party, a ballroom of people with signs in their hands and their mouths open, and the noise of it comes out of the little speaker like surf. Back at the desk the anchors say he has carried the city across its lines, Black neighborhoods and white.

“A Landrieu is a Landrieu,” Tony says, happy and loud, and pops the dish towel against the counter. “First white mayor since his daddy, and his daddy left in seventy-eight. This town’s been Black most of my life, and it went for him two to one. Look at that, son. Look at that.”

Jack looks at it. Tony said the first part the way a man gives the weather and the rest of it proud, and Jack can’t tell yet how the two halves fit together, in Tony or at the kitchen table on Glenwood Avenue, where he has heard men say *the city* and mean a map. He takes the head off a crawfish and puts the tail in the bowl.
“He gets the department how it is,” Luc says, from the counter. “With the federal cases.” That is all he says. Tony looks at him and turns back to the screen.

“I’m glad he won,” Lena says. She has a tail between her fingers and is pointing it at the television. “I am. I’m saying it in this kitchen, Daddy, mark it down.” She peels it. “But the city that voted tonight isn’t the city that was here in 2005. There are a hundred thousand people from this city in somebody’s cousin’s house in Houston who’d have had a say.”
“So they come home,” Jack says. “Make it safe enough to come home to. Fix the police, fix the schools —”
“Come home to *what*, Youngstown? You can’t come home to a slab.”
“Two-thirds is two-thirds. In Ohio that’s a landslide.”
“In Youngstown two-thirds is how many people moved to Charlotte.”
“That’s low.”
“That’s *demographics*.”

It goes fast, and it goes the old way: she knows the Corps of Engineers and the city council and which priest said what from which pulpit; he knows the steel towns and who left them and what the men who stayed elected after; same Creed, same Mass in the morning, opposite conclusions, and both of them peeling right through it without missing a tail. He had forgotten it had a speed. Tony stands over them with the dish towel and eggs them on, “Go ’head, cher,” and then, “Ohio, you going to take that?” At the counter something happens at one corner of Luc’s mouth and is put away again.
From the doorway, Mémère: “Y’all fight like married people.”
Not one of them corrects it fast enough. Lena puts a tail in the bowl. Jack puts a tail in the bowl. On the screen somebody throws confetti.

choices.text: “A city’s the people who come back. He won the people who came back.”
choices.key: At the Broussards’ kitchen table Landrieu won outright. You told Lena a city is the people who come back. She asked about the ones who couldn’t.
response: “And the ones who couldn’t?” Lena says. She is smiling down at the bowl when she says it. He has an answer for that, and she has one for his answer, and it goes round twice more, quicker each time, past the point and out the other side, with no hurry on either side to win it.
Tony, who lost the thread two rounds ago and is loving it anyway, reaches behind him and turns the television up so he can hear the anchors over the two of them.

choices.text: “I’d take anybody who fixes the cops. I don’t care who his father was.”
choices.key: At the Broussards’ kitchen table Landrieu won outright. You said you’d take anybody who fixes the cops. Luc looked at you a long second.
response: Luc looks at him a long second from the counter, and says nothing.

Lena’s eyes go from her brother to Jack and back, and she lets that one go, and takes the argument somewhere else, the schools, the levee board, anywhere. Tony, who missed all of it, turns the television up on the confetti.

choices.text: “You’re right about Houston. I didn’t think about who isn’t here.”
choices.key: At the Broussards’ kitchen table Landrieu won outright. You told Lena she was right about the people who aren’t here to vote.
response: She stops with her mouth open, ready for a fight that isn’t coming.

She shuts it. She peels the next tail and puts it in his bowl instead of hers. “Well, I don’t concede nothing,” Tony announces, and takes up the fight himself, Tony against the Corps of Engineers, the levee board and the city of Houston, and turns the television up to back himself.

choices.text: “In Youngstown we elected a congressman who went to prison, and he ran again from prison.”
choices.key: At the Broussards’ kitchen table Landrieu won outright. You told the table about Traficant running for Congress from prison. Tony was delighted.
response: Tony is delighted. He takes the dish towel off his shoulder to be delighted properly. “Your daddy vote for him?”

Tony laughs until he has to hold the counter, and Lena says Louisiana could field a team of those, and Tony says not in *this* kitchen, and they are off again, the three of them, while Tony turns the television up so the anchors can hear it too.
